title: Speeding up justice in Maguindanao massacre
primary_topics: The structural obstacles to speeding up the Maguindanao massacre trial after two years
CJ's call for a more gutsy prosecution and zealous defense to prevent witness attrition and delays
Judge Reyes as the trial's indispensable institutional anchor -- and the risk of her midstream transfer

stances.claim: The prosecution must be more gutsy in preparing more witnesses per trial day despite logistical challenges — the risks of delay (witness attrition, corruption, disappearance, death) far outweigh the operational difficulties of accelerating the testimony schedule.
stances.rhetorical_move: cost-of-delay argument: the temporal risks of judicial delay as the decisive consideration against the prosecution's operational objections

stances.claim: The defense should also want speed: 187 accused detained on capital charges may include innocent individuals who are suffering punishment without having been convicted — their interest in a prompt verdict is as strong as the prosecution's interest in securing it.
stances.rhetorical_move: innocent-detainee argument: the defense's own self-interest in avoiding protracted detention as a structural inducement for accelerating the trial

stances.claim: Judge Reyes must not be transferred or promoted midstream: she is the case's irreplaceable institutional anchor because her continuous observation of witness demeanor is a legal advantage that no transcript can replicate — and her fierce resolve is the trial's moral engine.
stances.rhetorical_move: continuity-of-observation argument: the legal doctrine of trial court primacy in credibility assessment as the institutional basis for preserving Judge Reyes

notable_anecdotes: The 'back-hoeing' of bodies — the most graphic detail in the column's opening — used not as sensationalism but as the moral baseline that gives urgency to every procedural obstacle: each delay in the trial is a delay in justice for 57 victims whose bodies were buried by a backhoe.

Judge Reyes's promotion risk: she may lose her chance to be promoted to the Sandiganbayan or CA because of the time consumed by this one case — CJ frames this as an institutional design flaw where judicial ambition and justice for massacre victims are placed in structural conflict.

The defense's 187 potential lawyers — 'each of whom is theoretically entitled to a lawyer who in turn may have different strategies' — as the most concrete illustration of how the size of the accused class transforms a single criminal case into a logistical and procedural nightmare with unlimited obstruction potential.

one_paragraph_summary: Two years after the November 23, 2009 Maguindanao massacre -- the senseless 'shooting, mangling and back-hoeing' of 57 civilians (32 journalists), allegedly masterminded by the Ampatuan clan and carried out by 187 accused -- Panganiban analyzes the obstacles to speeding up the trial. Judge Jocelyn Solis-Reyes recently directed the prosecution to prepare 5-6 witnesses per trial day and hear the case three times weekly (from the current twice weekly), but prosecutors balked: witnesses must be transported from Maguindanao, speak only local dialects, need personal reassurance of safety, and require government resources for housing and feeding. CJ argues that time is the prosecution's enemy -- witnesses forget, lose interest, become corruptible, disappear, or die -- and that 'a little more diligence, patience, and gutsiness' is essential. He also flags three structural risks: Judge Reyes's potential promotion would deny the trial the irreplaceable demeanor-observation advantage she has built over two years (the basic rule being that trial courts' credibility findings deserve great weight because they observe witnesses on the stand); the 187 accused each theoretically entitled to a lawyer with different strategies creates unlimited obstruction potential; and any interlocutory ruling could trigger a TRO from a higher court. He notes the defense should also want speed -- capital offense plus detention punishes potentially innocent accuseds -- and closes by applauding Judge Reyes's 'fierce resolve' to see that 'justice be done though the heavens may fall' (fiat justitia ruat caelum), deserving the support of both prosecution and defense and the eternal vigilance of the Filipino people.
